name: Fatima Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and became junior manager of a purchasing helpdesk in a large company four months ago. I have a bachelor's degree and supervise four people, but I still check difficult item codes with senior buyer Hana. We clear held orders for schools and other customers. I like the moment a missing box arrives; I dislike telling a school an order is complete when the paper is only complete on our screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household relying on just now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a lab technician, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My manager pay is typical for the role, we have about two months of expenses saved, and there are some similar posts nearby. I use AI now and then to draft a message, after checking the order myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our purchasing desk that a little automatic sorting could clear the easy requests, but a supplier still needs an answer when an order is held. I wouldn't call a shorter queue a better service unless the schools we supply actually get what they ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI sometimes to draft a supplier email, then check every item code myself. I became the junior team manager four months ago, and my partner's lab technician wage is steady, but the mortgage, two school-age children and only two months of savings keep me alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This Thursday I'll keep checking the held orders against the purchase request and use AI only to draft the plain status messages. In the first year of the plateau, we'll add 100 a month to cash after the mortgage and school meals are paid, and I'll ask my experienced buyer to show me why our worst orders got stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the small routine changes because I'm still learning the team. The household is paying its bills, but two months of cash isn't a long rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which order got stuck last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school supply order had two item codes for the same box of paper, and the program flagged one as a duplicate. My senior buyer Hana spotted that one code was for the recycled stock before we cancelled the wrong line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the extra 100 isn't there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We won't force it; the mortgage and school meals get paid first. I'd rather put 40 away honestly than label a transfer that bounces.

say: I'd welcome **simple sorting** if suppliers still get a human answer on held orders.
I'd judge the tool by **delivered supplies**, not the queue length.
think: I use **AI drafts** sometimes, but I still check item codes myself.
Two months saved and a mortgage keep me **alert**, even with my partner's steady wage.
do: Check **held orders** against purchase requests and draft only plain status messages with AI.
Add **100 monthly** to cash after mortgage and school meals if available; learn why bad orders stuck from Hana.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about learning the manager role with only two months saved.
S0.quote: I'd rather put 40 away honestly than label a transfer that bounces.
fieldNote: She ties a small automation gain to **actual school deliveries**, not dashboard speed.
The cash goal is **conditional after mortgage**, with a smaller amount acceptable when the full 100 is unavailable.

steps.text: Check held school supply orders against original purchase requests
Add up to 100 monthly to cash after mortgage and school meals when available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the buying team Steady Disruption will take over routine orders, supplier emails and many price checks, so we need to see which exceptions still need us. I would support a trial only if our branch can compare the software with the current buyers' decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am new to managing and not yet quick with complicated supplier terms. If head office gives one manager two teams, my post could be folded away; two months of cash and a mortgage make that more than a career inconvenience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask Hana to pick twenty past purchase disputes and test the new tool on copies while I learn its exception screen. In the first year of disruption, if the test catches the wrong item codes and the company pays for training time, I'd take the buyer systems course; if my management post is merged, I'd apply for a buyer role only where the pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the manager title, but I can work through a controlled trial. I don't want my team graded on a program we haven't checked ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the trial passed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must catch all the wrong item codes in Hana's twenty examples and show a person how to reverse a bad hold. One missed delivery to a school is a real problem, not a pretty percentage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a buyer role for less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after my partner and I do the mortgage and childcare sums. There are a few buyer jobs nearby. A vacancy is not an offer and a lower title doesn't automatically mean a lower wage.

say: I'd support a **twenty-case trial** before software replaces routine orders and emails.
I'd ask which **supplier exceptions** still need people to fix them.
think: A two-team manager arrangement could remove my **new post**.
Two months saved and the **mortgage** make a loss of manager pay serious.
do: Test **twenty old disputes** with Hana and learn the exception screen this month.
Take **paid systems training** if the trial passes; seek buyer work only if wages cover mortgage and childcare.
feel: She feels **anxious** about her post, though a checked trial gives her something to do.
S1.quote: A vacancy is not an offer and a lower title doesn't automatically mean a lower wage.
fieldNote: Her **all-codes threshold** links the trial to school supplies rather than an abstract accuracy score.
She separates a **possible vacancy** from a real offer and checks pay with her partner before moving.

steps.text: Learn the new exception screen on twenty copied purchase disputes
Apply for nearby buyer posts after merger only if wages cover mortgage and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff AGI by 2028 can plan and buy nearly everything on our screens, and head office must say which people will still sign off held orders. I would ask for a dated staffing plan and someone who can override a wrong supplier choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work reaches my desk in 2028, while robots around 2031 are a separate issue for physical deliveries. I expect head office might remove our junior manager layer; with two months saved, we could keep the mortgage current for a short time but not through a long job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll put our mortgage and school costs on one page with my partner, request the staffing date, and prepare three examples where a human saved a school order. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd compare its held-order decisions with those examples if still employed; if my post ends, I'd apply to nearby supply offices only where an actual vacancy has viable pay and hours, keeping our home until a signed offer is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about having two months to find another paycheck. I can test a tool, but I cannot make a school bill wait because a company needs another meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for the children first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the paid music lessons, 55 a month, if my salary ended and ask the teacher whether the school has a free place. I wouldn't tell the children to give up music while I still have a paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help if your search took longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's sister could collect the children after school for a few weeks if I had interviews out of town. I'd ask only when a real interview is booked; I don't want to build a plan out of her unpaid time.

say: I'd seek a **dated staffing plan** and a person able to override wrong supplier choices.
I'd tell staff **screen buying work** changes in 2028, before delivery robots arrive.
think: My **junior layer** could go as AGI reaches buying and planning in 2028.
Two months saved cover the **mortgage briefly**, not a long search for another manager post.
do: List **mortgage and school costs** now and request a staffing date.
After 2028, test **held-order decisions** if employed; apply only for real vacancies with viable pay and hours if cut.
feel: She feels **alarmed** by the short time her savings could replace her wage.
S2.quote: I wouldn't tell the children to give up music while I still have a paycheck.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a **2028 screen shock** from physical delivery robots expected around 2031.
Music fees and family childcare are **conditional fallbacks**, triggered only by job loss or a real out-of-town interview.

steps.text: Test AGI held-order decisions against three past examples after 2028 if employed
Apply for nearby supply vacancies only if pay and hours work after post ends
Stop 55 monthly music fees only if her salary ends
Ask partner sister for childcare only when an out-of-town interview is booked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2031 gives us five years to learn the hard supplier cases and to ask where the real buyer openings will be. I want training tied to a list of jobs, not a certificate hung above a shrinking desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me become a stronger buyer while our children get older and our mortgage balance falls. My ordering and checking work still changes in 2031; buyer jobs are screen work too, so that route might shrink as well. Robots around 2034 could change physical delivery, but they do not lengthen my desk deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring, if our company pays for time, I'd take its contract-terms workshop and practise negotiating two disputed supplier deliveries with Hana watching. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek an internal buyer vacancy if one exists; otherwise I'd apply to the regional purchasing office only after checking its pay and school-compatible hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about needing a new route, but five years is time to earn it. I would not tell my family the workshop is a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes those two disputes useful practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One was a late school delivery and the other a price rise after an order was approved. I'd need to call the suppliers, hear what they could actually do, and document what they agreed; that part still makes me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why school-compatible hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner sometimes works a late lab shift, and I collect our younger child. A post with evening calls every day would require paid childcare, so we'd price that before I applied.

say: I'd ask for **real buyer openings** alongside training before 2031.
I'd tell staff to learn **supplier disputes**, not collect certificates for disappearing desks.
think: Five years could make me a **stronger buyer** before my screen work changes.
The **2034 robot date** concerns deliveries, not my 2031 buying deadline.
do: Take a **paid contract workshop** next spring if the company funds time; practise two supplier calls.
Seek an **internal buyer vacancy** after 2031, or regional work only after pay and school hours check.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about changing routes but able to practise over five years.
S3.quote: I would not tell my family the workshop is a job offer.
fieldNote: The training is **own negotiation practice** on two real disputes, conditional on company-paid time.
Any outside move must fit **school pickup** and paid childcare costs, not just a higher title.

steps.text: Take contract-terms workshop if company pays and practise two supplier calls
Apply for internal buyer vacancy after 2031 if one exists
Apply regionally if no internal role and pay plus school hours work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make fair changes in purchasing, if head office lets junior staff handle real supplier calls now. I would ask for a yearly list of roles and paid practice days so people can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 then, and the children might be through school, but I won't assume the mortgage is gone. I could spend the decade learning how to settle supply failures, though AGI could handle parts of that thinking work by 2036 too. Robots around 2039 will not protect the supplier calls; I do not want to stay the person who only approves an AI form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep checking held orders and ask to sit with Hana on one supplier call a month, taking the calls if suppliers agree. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay if I still resolve real supply failures at a wage that covers our mortgage; if the role becomes button pressing, I'd apply to other offices with vacancies while still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about wasting the time, not terrified by the date. The current mortgage still makes each pay review matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your family afford a slower promotion path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes if both our wages hold and we keep paying the mortgage on time, but we'd pause the idea of a larger home. A bigger house is a wish, not a promise to the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Hana to let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to make the first call when a delivery fails, with Hana beside me, and write the supplier's answer myself. If I still need my senior buyer to make every hard call in ten years, I haven't really learned the job.

say: I'd seek **yearly role lists** and paid practice days across the decade.
I'd ask for **real supplier calls** for junior staff before 2036.
think: At **53**, school costs may ease, but the mortgage may remain.
I need to settle **real supply failures**, not only approve machine forms.
do: Keep **checking held orders** and join monthly supplier calls if suppliers agree.
After 2036, stay for **mortgage-covering work** with real decisions; seek other openings while employed if reduced to buttons.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about wasting time, while current mortgage payments still weigh on her.
S4.quote: If I still need my senior buyer to make every hard call in ten years, I haven't really learned the job.
fieldNote: The long runway gives her **monthly call practice**, but the mortgage still rules out a casual pay drop.
Her household's larger-home wish stays **conditional**, while the present home remains the priority.

steps.text: Keep checking held purchase orders this year
Join one supplier call monthly if the supplier agrees
Apply to other offices after 2036 if role loses decisions, without resigning first

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the purchasing desk could shrink before I have learned to handle the hardest supplier calls. A dated staffing plan, paid time with experienced buyers, and a real role with mortgage-covering pay would help me plan for our children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who answers a school when a program calls a needed box a duplicate. The order is finished only when the right supplies reach the door.

headlineQuote: The order is finished only when the right supplies reach the door.
portrait: At **43**, Fatima is a new purchasing helpdesk manager who still checks difficult item codes with a senior buyer.
Her **two-month cushion**, mortgage and school costs limit risk despite two steady wages and some local roles.
She uses **AI occasionally**, testing it on old cases before trusting it with supplier decisions.
Fast AGI threatens her **junior post**; longer runways let her practise supplier calls if funded and vacancies exist.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her purchasing wage before she learns the supplier work that might remain.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing date**, paid buyer practice and a mortgage-covering vacancy would give her family a workable option.
